questions.question: Which statement explains why L-DOPA can treat Parkinson disease (options: acts on a different receptor; crosses blood-brain barrier then converted to dopamine in brain; converted to dopamine in blood then crosses; identical to dopamine)?
questions.answer: B L-DOPA crosses the blood-brain barrier and is then converted to dopamine in the brain
steps: Dopamine itself cannot cross the blood-brain barrier.
L-DOPA is small enough to cross and is then converted into dopamine by enzymes in the brain.
Options A, C and D are incorrect, so B is correct.

questions.question: Explain why releasing reduced quantities of dopamine by presynaptic neurones could result in motor symptoms.
questions.answer: Less dopamine crosses the synapse, so fewer post-synaptic receptors are stimulated and movement control is impaired.
steps: Dopamine is released from the presynaptic neurone into the synaptic cleft.
Less dopamine means fewer dopamine molecules bind to receptors on the post-synaptic membrane.
Fewer post-synaptic responses in the motor pathway (basal ganglia) disrupt control of muscle movement.
This imbalance causes the tremors and rigidity seen in Parkinson disease.

questions.question: Suggest how the release of dopamine from presynaptic neurones could be inhibited.
questions.answer: Block voltage-gated calcium channels on the presynaptic membrane so Ca2+ cannot enter and trigger vesicle fusion.
steps: Dopamine release is triggered by Ca2+ entering the presynaptic neurone through voltage-gated channels.
A drug that blocks these calcium channels prevents Ca2+ entry.
Without Ca2+, synaptic vesicles do not fuse with the membrane, so exocytosis of dopamine is inhibited.

questions.topic: Microarrays And Bioinformatics In Disease Genetics
questions.question: Describe how microarrays and bioinformatics could be used to investigate the genetic basis of Parkinson disease.
questions.answer: Microarrays compare gene expression in affected and healthy neurones, and bioinformatics analyses the data to find candidate genes.
steps: Extract mRNA from dopamine neurones of affected and unaffected individuals and make labelled cDNA.
Hybridise the cDNA to a microarray carrying probes for thousands of genes and measure fluorescence.
Use bioinformatics software to compare expression levels and find genes that differ significantly.
Compare the candidate sequences with genome databases to identify mutations or variants linked to the disease.

questions.question: Explain why mutations in the RPE65 gene can result in blindness.
questions.answer: A mutation changes the enzyme RPE65, so trans-retinal is not converted to cis-retinal and rhodopsin cannot form to detect light.
steps: A mutation changes the base sequence of the RPE65 gene, altering the amino acid sequence.
The altered enzyme has a changed shape, so its active site cannot convert trans-retinal to cis-retinal.
Without cis-retinal, rhodopsin (opsin plus retinal) cannot be formed in rod cells.
Light cannot be detected and transmitted to the brain, so the person is blind.

questions.question: Describe how genes that cause blindness, when mutated, could be identified.
questions.answer: Sequence DNA of affected and unaffected individuals and use bioinformatics to find shared mutations in candidate genes.
steps: Collect DNA from affected and unaffected family members or a population.
Sequence the genomes or candidate genes, or use microarrays to compare gene expression in retinal cells.
Use bioinformatics to find mutations or expression differences that are present only in affected people.
Confirm the link with further experiments, such as gene knockout or gene therapy studies.

questions.question: Describe how genetic engineering could be used to produce rice that contains beta-carotene.
questions.answer: Isolate the beta-carotene gene from soil bacteria, insert it into a vector with a promoter, transfer it into rice cells, and select transformed plants.
steps: Isolate the carotenoid (beta-carotene) gene from the soil bacteria, using restriction enzymes or reverse transcription from mRNA.
Use the same restriction enzyme to cut a plasmid vector and join the gene in with DNA ligase, including a promoter and a marker gene.
Transfer the recombinant plasmid into rice cells, for example by Agrobacterium or a gene gun.
Select transformed cells using the marker gene, then regenerate whole rice plants that express beta-carotene.

questions.question: Describe the possible risks of growing genetically modified rice plants.
questions.answer: Risks include gene transfer to wild relatives, harm to other organisms or biodiversity, spread of antibiotic-resistance marker genes, and unknown allergic or health effects.
steps: Pollen from GM rice could cross-pollinate wild relatives, transferring the new genes into wild populations.
The new genes could reduce biodiversity or harm non-target organisms such as insects.
Marker genes for antibiotic resistance could be transferred to bacteria.
Unknown long-term effects on human health, such as allergies, may occur.

questions.question: Suggest how one of these risks could be reduced.
questions.answer: Use male-sterile GM rice or plant buffer zones to stop pollen spreading genes to wild relatives.
steps: Male-sterile plants cannot release viable pollen, so genes cannot spread to wild relatives.
Alternatively, grow a buffer zone of non-GM plants around the field to reduce cross-pollination.

questions.question: Compare and contrast fMRI and CT scans used to identify structures such as plaques in the brain.
questions.answer: Both are non-invasive imaging methods; CT uses X-rays for structure, while fMRI uses magnetic fields and blood oxygen changes to show activity.
steps: Both methods produce images of the brain without surgery.
CT uses X-rays and gives a detailed structural image, but is less sensitive for soft-tissue detail.
fMRI uses strong magnetic fields and radio waves and detects changes in blood oxygenation to show brain activity.
fMRI gives better soft-tissue contrast and functional information, while CT is quicker and cheaper for structural detail.

questions.topic: Showing Bacterial Genetic Material Is Active
questions.question: Describe how the team could show that the genetic material from P. gingivalis in the cerebral cortex is active.
questions.answer: Extract RNA from the cortex, reverse transcribe it and use PCR to detect bacterial mRNA transcripts, showing the genes are transcribed.
steps: Extract total RNA from the cerebral cortex samples.
Carry out reverse transcription to make cDNA from the mRNA.
Use PCR or qPCR with primers specific to P. gingivalis genes to detect the transcripts.
Detection of mRNA (not just DNA) shows the genes are being transcribed, so they are active; compare with control samples.

questions.question: Suggest how the genes affected by toxicants can be identified.
questions.answer: Compare mRNA levels in exposed and unexposed cells using microarrays or RNA-seq, then use bioinformatics to find genes with altered expression.
steps: Expose cells to the toxicant and keep control cells unexposed.
Extract mRNA from both sets and use microarrays or RNA sequencing to measure expression of each gene.
Use bioinformatics to identify genes whose expression changes significantly.

questions.topic: Homology Between Human And Zebrafish Genes
questions.question: Explain how scientists could determine the high degree of homology of genes between humans and zebrafish.
questions.answer: Compare the DNA or amino acid sequences of the genes using bioinformatics (e.g. BLAST) and count the percentage of identical bases or amino acids.
steps: Obtain the gene sequences for the same gene in humans and zebrafish from databases.
Align the sequences using bioinformatics software such as BLAST.
Count identical bases or amino acids to calculate percentage similarity.
High similarity shows the genes share a common ancestor and are conserved through evolution.

questions.question: Suggest how electrophilic species (ES) and free radicals could be involved in modulating gene expression.
questions.answer: ES can covalently modify transcription factors or histone proteins, changing their activity and so altering which genes are expressed.
steps: ES are reactive molecules that can form covalent bonds with nucleophilic groups (such as cysteine residues) on proteins.
Binding to transcription factors can change their shape and their ability to bind DNA.
Changes to histones or other regulatory proteins alter chromatin structure, switching gene expression on or off.

questions.question: Suggest how electrophilic species (ES) can damage mitochondrial DNA.
questions.answer: ES react with mtDNA bases to form adducts, causing mutations and strand damage; mtDNA lacks histones and has limited repair.
steps: ES are reactive and form covalent adducts with the bases of mtDNA.
These adducts block DNA replication and transcription and cause mutations.
mtDNA is near the electron transport chain where free radicals are produced and has few histones or repair systems, so it is vulnerable.

questions.topic: Using MTT Assay To Compare Toxicity
questions.question: Describe how the MTT assay could be used to show which of two drugs is more toxic to cells.
questions.answer: Expose cells to each drug, add MTT, measure the purple colour (absorbance); less purple means fewer viable cells, so more toxic.
steps: Culture the same number of cells and treat them with each drug at the same concentration, with an untreated control.
Add MTT; living cells with reduced NAD produce NADH-dependent reduction, changing yellow MTT to purple formazan.
Measure the absorbance of each sample with a colorimeter (spectrophotometer).
Lower absorbance (less purple) means fewer viable cells, so the drug with the lower reading is more toxic.

questions.question: Explain the advantages of reprogramming ordinary somatic cells to behave like embryonic stem cells for stem cell-based assays of toxicants.
questions.answer: Reprogrammed cells avoid the ethical issues of using embryos and can be made from the same individual, giving many cell types for testing.
steps: Induced pluripotent stem cells can be made from adult cells without using embryos, avoiding ethical concerns.
They can be made from many individuals, including patients, so tests reflect genetic variation.
They can differentiate into many cell types, so toxicants can be tested on relevant tissues.

questions.question: Describe how light is detected by rod cells in the eye.
questions.answer: Light changes retinal from cis to trans, activating rhodopsin and a G-protein cascade that closes Na+ channels and hyperpolarises the rod.
steps: Light is absorbed by rhodopsin (opsin plus cis-retinal) in the rod outer segment.
Cis-retinal changes shape to trans-retinal, which activates the opsin protein.
This activates a G-protein and phosphodiesterase cascade that lowers cGMP levels.
cGMP-gated Na+ channels close, so the rod hyperpolarises and less neurotransmitter is released to the bipolar cell.

questions.topic: Identifying Genes Expressed In Sensory Neurones
questions.question: Suggest how the genes expressed in a sensory neurone could be identified.
questions.answer: Extract mRNA from sensory neurones and use RNA-seq or microarrays, with RT-PCR or in situ hybridisation to confirm specific genes.
steps: Isolate sensory neurones and extract their mRNA.
Use microarrays or RNA sequencing to identify which genes are transcribed.
Compare with other cell types to find genes specific to sensory neurones.
Confirm individual genes with RT-PCR or in situ hybridisation.

questions.question: Explain how capsaicin could activate nerve cells causing a pain sensation.
questions.answer: Capsaicin binds to the TRPV1 ion channel, which opens and lets Na+ and Ca2+ in, depolarising the nerve cell to fire an action potential.
steps: Capsaicin binds to the TRPV1 receptor-channel on the sensory nerve membrane.
The channel opens, allowing Na+ and Ca2+ to flow into the neurone down their gradients.
The membrane depolarises to threshold, generating an action potential.
The impulse travels to the brain and is perceived as pain.

questions.topic: Ion Channel Changes And Nerve Impulses
questions.question: Explain how changes in an ion channel protein can result in nerve impulses in the nervous system.
questions.answer: A change in the channel protein opens it, letting Na+ in, which depolarises the membrane to threshold and triggers an action potential.
steps: The ion channel protein changes shape, opening its pore.
Na+ ions flow into the neurone down their electrochemical gradient.
The membrane depolarises; if it reaches threshold, an action potential is generated and travels along the neurone.

questions.question: Explain how mechanical stimuli such as pressure are converted into electrical signals in cells.
questions.answer: Pressure stretches mechanosensitive Piezo ion channels, opening them so cations enter and depolarise the cell (receptor potential).
steps: Pressure stretches the cell membrane and the attached mechanosensitive ion channel (e.g. Piezo).
The channel opens, allowing Na+ and Ca2+ to flow into the cell.
This depolarisation (receptor potential) reaches threshold and triggers action potentials in the sensory neurone.

questions.question: Explain what is meant by the phrase "based on its similarity to Piezo 1, a second ion channel was found (Piezo 2)".
questions.answer: Scientists searched genomes for DNA sequences similar to the Piezo 1 gene and found a related gene encoding a second channel (Piezo 2).
steps: Piezo 1 is a known mechanosensitive ion channel.
Scientists used bioinformatics to search genome databases for genes with similar DNA sequences.
The matching gene was found to code for another channel, Piezo 2, with a related structure and probably a similar function.

questions.topic: Role Of TRPV1 In Temperature Maintenance
questions.question: Suggest the role of TRPV1 in maintaining core body temperature.
questions.answer: TRPV1 is a heat-sensitive ion channel that detects high temperature and triggers responses such as sweating and vasodilation to lose heat.
steps: TRPV1 opens when temperature rises above about 43 degrees C in thermoreceptor neurones.
Signals reach the hypothalamus, which triggers heat loss responses such as sweating and vasodilation.

questions.topic: Genetically Modifying Sheep For rHE In Milk
questions.question: Explain how a sheep could be genetically modified to produce rHE in its milk.
questions.answer: Insert the human erythropoietin gene next to a mammary-specific promoter, inject it into a fertilised egg, and breed sheep that secrete rHE in milk.
steps: Isolate the human erythropoietin gene from cDNA made from mRNA, or using restriction enzymes.
Insert the gene into a vector with a promoter that is active only in mammary gland cells, plus a marker gene.
Inject the construct into a fertilised sheep egg (zygote) and implant it into a surrogate ewe.
Breed transgenic sheep and select those whose milk contains rHE, then collect and purify the protein.

questions.question: Calculate the percentage increase in mean blood haemoglobin from 80 to 142 g dm-3 after rHE treatment.

Percentage increase = 62 / 80 x 100 = 77.5 %.

questions.question: Describe how anti-rHE antibodies may be produced in some patients receiving rHE.
questions.answer: rHE acts as a foreign antigen; B cells with matching receptors are activated with T helper cells and divide into plasma cells that secrete antibodies.
steps: rHE is a foreign protein, so it acts as an antigen in the patient.
B lymphocytes with receptors complementary to the rHE antigen bind it, and T helper cells release cytokines to activate them.
Clonal selection leads to clonal expansion, forming plasma cells and memory cells.
Plasma cells secrete anti-rHE antibodies that bind rHE and mark it for destruction.

questions.question: Explain why Co-beneldopa is more effective than L-dopa alone in treating Parkinson disease.
questions.answer: The second drug stops L-dopa being converted to dopamine in the blood, so more L-dopa crosses into the brain to be converted there.
steps: L-dopa given alone is largely converted to dopamine in the blood (peripheral tissues).
Dopamine made in the blood cannot cross the blood-brain barrier, so less reaches the brain.
Co-beneldopa blocks this peripheral conversion, so more L-dopa crosses into the brain.
More dopamine is made in the brain, improving symptoms and reducing side effects of high blood dopamine.

questions.topic: Volume Of Air Entering Alveoli Per Hour
questions.question: Calculate the volume of air entering the alveoli each hour, given tidal volume 500 cm3, dead space 150 cm3 and respiratory rate 12 breaths per minute, to 2 s.f.
questions.answer: 2.5 x 10^5 cm3 per hour
steps: Air reaching alveoli per breath = VT - DS = 500 - 150 = 350 cm3.
Per minute = 350 x 12 = 4200 cm3 min-1.
Per hour = 4200 x 60 = 252 000 cm3 h-1, which is 2.5 x 10^5 cm3 h-1 (2 s.f.).

questions.question: Suggest why there is a relationship between the ageing process and neurodegeneration.
questions.answer: With age, mitochondria accumulate ROS damage and mtDNA mutations, so energy supply to neurones falls and neurones die.
steps: Ageing leads to accumulation of mutations and damage in mitochondria.
Reactive oxygen species damage mtDNA and proteins, reducing oxidative phosphorylation.
Reduced ATP supply makes neurones more vulnerable to death, causing neurodegeneration.

questions.topic: Energy From Glucose In Oxidative Phosphorylation
questions.question: Describe how energy released from glucose is used in oxidative phosphorylation.
questions.answer: Electrons from NADH and FADH2 pass down the electron transport chain, pumping protons to make a gradient that drives ATP synthase.
steps: Reduced NAD and FAD (from glycolysis, link reaction and Krebs cycle) donate electrons to the electron transport chain.
Energy from the electrons is used to pump protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space.
Protons flow back through ATP synthase, driving synthesis of ATP from ADP and Pi (chemiosmosis).
Oxygen is the final electron acceptor, forming water.

questions.question: Explain how free radicals (reactive oxygen species) can cause damage to mitochondrial DNA.
questions.answer: ROS oxidise mtDNA bases and cause strand breaks; mtDNA has no histones and limited repair, so mutations accumulate.
steps: ROS such as superoxide and hydroxyl radicals are produced as leaks from the electron transport chain.
ROS react with and oxidise DNA bases, causing base changes and strand breaks.
mtDNA lacks protective histones and has limited repair, so the damage accumulates as mutations.

questions.question: Describe how the differentiation of highly specialised brain cells can occur.
questions.answer: Differentiation occurs when different sets of genes are switched on or off by transcription factors and epigenetic control.
steps: All cells in an organism contain the same genome.
During development, different transcription factors and signals switch on different genes in each cell.
Only a subset of genes is expressed, leading to different proteins and cell structures.
These specialised cells then have the morphology and function suited to their role.

questions.question: Explain what is meant by the phrase "mitochondrial proteome".
questions.answer: The complete set of proteins present in mitochondria, encoded by both nuclear and mitochondrial genes.
steps: Proteome means all the proteins in a cell or organelle.
The mitochondrial proteome includes proteins coded by nuclear DNA and by mtDNA.

questions.question: Explain why synaptic mitochondria are more susceptible to ageing than mitochondria in other parts of a neurone.
questions.answer: Synapses have very high energy demand and handle large Ca2+ fluxes, producing more ROS that damage synaptic mitochondria.
steps: Synaptic terminals have a high and fluctuating energy demand for neurotransmitter release and recycling.
High activity and Ca2+ handling in these mitochondria produce more ROS.
This damages the mitochondria and mtDNA more quickly, so they age faster.

questions.question: Explain why the mitochondrial genome is essential for oxidative phosphorylation.
questions.answer: mtDNA codes for several subunits of the electron transport chain complexes and the rRNA and tRNA needed to make them.
steps: mtDNA encodes some of the polypeptide subunits of the electron transport chain complexes.
It also encodes mitochondrial rRNA and tRNA needed to synthesise these proteins inside the mitochondria.

questions.question: Suggest how damaged mitochondria are removed by autophagy.
questions.answer: Damaged mitochondria are tagged, engulfed in an autophagosome, which fuses with a lysosome so hydrolytic enzymes digest them.
steps: Damaged mitochondria are tagged for removal (e.g. with ubiquitin).
They are engulfed by a double-membrane autophagosome.
The autophagosome fuses with a lysosome, and hydrolytic enzymes digest the mitochondria.

questions.question: Describe how a neurotransmitter allows an impulse to be transferred to an adjacent neurone.
questions.answer: An action potential causes Ca2+ entry, vesicles release the neurotransmitter, which binds receptors and depolarises the next neurone.
steps: An action potential arrives at the presynaptic knob and opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels.
Ca2+ entry causes vesicles to fuse with the membrane and release neurotransmitter by exocytosis.
The neurotransmitter diffuses across the synaptic cleft and binds to receptors on the post-synaptic membrane.
Ion channels open, depolarising the post-synaptic neurone so an action potential is generated if threshold is reached.

steps: Restriction endonucleases cut DNA at specific palindromic sequences.
They produce sticky ends that allow the gene to be inserted into a vector.

questions.question: Where is DNA found in a bacterial cell (options: nucleus only; plasmid only; plasmid and cytoplasm; plasmid and nucleus)?
questions.answer: C plasmid and cytoplasm
steps: Bacteria have no nucleus, so option A and D are wrong.
Their main DNA is a circular chromosome in the nucleoid region of the cytoplasm, and plasmids are also in the cytoplasm.

questions.topic: Bond Joining Nucleotides In DNA Strand
questions.question: Which bond joins nucleotides together in a single strand of DNA (options: hydrogen, ionic, peptide, phosphodiester)?
questions.answer: D phosphodiester
steps: Adjacent nucleotides are joined by a bond between the sugar of one and the phosphate of the next.
This is a phosphodiester bond; hydrogen bonds join bases between strands.

questions.question: Describe how genes can be switched off by transcription factors.
questions.answer: Repressor transcription factors bind to DNA near the promoter and block RNA polymerase from binding or transcribing the gene.
steps: A repressor transcription factor binds to a specific sequence near the gene (e.g. a silencer or operator).
It blocks RNA polymerase from binding to the promoter or moving along the gene.
Transcription stops, so no mRNA and no protein are made from that gene.

questions.question: Explain the role of gut microorganisms in decomposing complex polysaccharides.
questions.answer: Gut bacteria secrete enzymes that hydrolyse glycosidic bonds in polysaccharides into monosaccharides and short-chain fatty acids that can be absorbed.
steps: Gut bacteria secrete extracellular enzymes such as cellulases and amylases.
These enzymes hydrolyse the glycosidic bonds in complex polysaccharides, breaking them into smaller sugars.
Monosaccharides and short-chain fatty acids produced can be absorbed and used by the host.

questions.question: Describe how the vagus nerve is involved in the control of heart rate.
questions.answer: The vagus nerve is parasympathetic and releases acetylcholine at the SAN, slowing heart rate.
steps: The cardiac control centre in the medulla oblongata sends impulses along the vagus nerve.
The vagus nerve releases acetylcholine onto the sinoatrial node (SAN).
Acetylcholine hyperpolarises SAN cells and slows the rate of depolarisation, decreasing heart rate.
This parasympathetic effect reduces heart rate when the body is at rest.

fMRI detects changes in blood oxygenation, which reflect neural activity in each region.
Compare the scans to see which memory and sensory regions show increased or decreased activity.

questions.topic: Diet, Gut Flora And Brain Chemicals
questions.question: Suggest how changes in diet could affect the composition of gut flora, causing imbalances in naturally occurring chemicals in the brain.
questions.answer: Diet changes the substrates available to gut bacteria, altering microbiota composition and their production of neurotransmitter precursors that signal to the brain.
steps: Diet supplies the food (substrates) that different gut bacteria use, so changes in diet alter microbial populations.
The balance of bacteria changes the amounts of metabolites such as short-chain fatty acids and neurotransmitter precursors produced.
These chemicals reach the brain via the blood and the vagus nerve, altering neurotransmitter levels such as serotonin.

questions.question: Explain how demyelination could result in poor coordination and loss of vision in multiple sclerosis.
questions.answer: Demyelination stops insulation of axons, so impulses slow or fail to reach muscles and the optic nerve.
steps: Myelin insulates axons and allows saltatory conduction, making impulses fast.
Demyelination slows or blocks impulse transmission along the axon.
Impulses to muscles are delayed (poor coordination) and impulses from the optic nerve are blocked (loss of vision).

Sequence the candidate gene and use bioinformatics to confirm it codes for a receptor.

questions.question: Explain how these neurotoxins prevent the generation of nerve impulses.
questions.answer: Inhibiting ACh release, blocking ion channels, or blocking ACh receptors each stops depolarisation of the post-synaptic membrane, so no action potential is generated.

Lower fluorescence for electron transport genes means they are downregulated, while higher fluorescence for the sirtuin gene means it is upregulated.

questions.question: Explain why Sudan Black was used in this study.
questions.answer: Sudan Black is a lipid stain that binds to fat, so the amount of fat stored in the nematodes can be seen and measured.
steps: Sudan Black is a fat-soluble dye that dissolves in and stains lipids.
Staining allows the fat stores in the nematodes to be seen and compared between groups.

questions.question: Describe how active genes could be identified.
questions.answer: Extract mRNA from cells, reverse transcribe it to cDNA and use microarrays or PCR to detect which genes are being transcribed.
steps: Extract mRNA from the cells, since only transcribed genes produce mRNA.
Reverse transcribe the mRNA into cDNA.
Use a microarray or RT-PCR to detect which cDNA sequences are present, showing active genes.

questions.question: Which is the role of histones in the cell (options: act as transcription factor; form pores in nuclear membrane; give structural support for DNA; produce RNA polymerase)?
questions.answer: C give structural support for DNA molecules
steps: Histones are proteins around which DNA is wound to form nucleosomes.
They provide structural support and help package DNA into chromatin.

questions.question: Which is the process that regulates gene expression (options: crossing over; epigenetic changes; post-transcriptional changes; post-translational changes)?
questions.answer: B epigenetic changes
steps: Epigenetic changes (e.g. methylation, histone modification) control whether genes are switched on or off.
Crossing over occurs in meiosis, not in gene regulation.

questions.question: Explain why these changes in the chromosomes of this individual would cause Prader-Willi syndrome.
questions.answer: The paternal copy is deleted and the maternal copy is methylated, so no functional genes from chromosome 15 are expressed.
steps: Some genes on chromosome 15 are expressed only from the paternal chromosome (imprinting).
The paternal copy has deletions, so these genes are missing.
The maternal copy is methylated and silenced, so none of the genes are expressed, causing the symptoms.

questions.question: Describe how Escherichia coli bacteria can be used to produce human growth hormone.
questions.answer: Insert the human growth hormone gene into a bacterial plasmid, transform E. coli, and culture them so they make and secrete the hormone for purification.
steps: Isolate the HGH gene by reverse transcribing HGH mRNA from pituitary cells to make cDNA.
Insert the cDNA into a plasmid vector with a promoter and marker gene using restriction enzymes and ligase.
Transform E. coli with the recombinant plasmid and select transformed bacteria using the marker.
Culture the bacteria in a fermenter so they express HGH, which is then extracted and purified.

questions.question: Describe the possible role of hypertension in causing dementia.
questions.answer: High blood pressure damages small brain blood vessels, reducing blood and oxygen supply and so causing neurone death and cognitive decline.
steps: Chronic high blood pressure damages the walls of small blood vessels in the brain.
Damaged vessels reduce blood flow and oxygen and glucose supply to neurones.
Starved neurones lose function and die, leading to cognitive decline (vascular dementia).

questions.question: Suggest why beta-amyloid is chemically sticky and gradually clumps together, using knowledge of protein structure.
questions.answer: Beta-amyloid contains hydrophobic amino acid R groups that stick together, and misfolded beta-sheet structures link to form aggregates.
steps: Beta-amyloid contains many hydrophobic amino acids whose R groups stick together in water.
It can fold into a misfolded beta-pleated sheet shape, which is stabilised by hydrogen bonds between chains.
These sticky interactions link molecules together, so they gradually clump into plaques.

questions.question: Describe the information that would be obtained from using a combined MRI and PET scan of the brain.
questions.answer: MRI gives detailed structural images while PET shows metabolic activity or amyloid deposits, so the two together show where activity and structure coincide.
steps: MRI shows detailed brain structure and any shrinkage in regions.
PET uses a radioactive tracer to show metabolic activity or the presence of amyloid plaques.
Combining them locates abnormal activity or plaques precisely within the brain structure.

questions.topic: Ethical Reason For Not Telling People At Risk
questions.question: State one reason why it might be considered unethical to tell people they are at risk of developing cognitive impairment.
questions.answer: It could cause anxiety and distress, especially if there is no effective treatment.
steps: Learning of a future risk can cause psychological distress and anxiety.
If there is no cure or effective treatment, the information offers no benefit.

questions.topic: Falling Blood Pressure And Brain Health
questions.question: Explain why a falling blood pressure might result in poor brain health.
questions.answer: Lower blood pressure reduces blood flow to the brain, so less oxygen and glucose reach neurones, reducing ATP and causing neurone damage.
steps: Blood pressure drives blood flow through the brain capillaries.
Falling pressure reduces blood flow, so less oxygen and glucose reach brain cells.
Without enough oxygen and glucose, aerobic respiration and ATP production fall, so neurones malfunction or die.

questions.question: Describe how scientists could identify the link between genes and the risk of dementia.
questions.answer: Compare the genomes of people with and without dementia, using genome-wide association studies and statistics to find variants linked to risk.
steps: Collect DNA from large groups of people with and without dementia.
Sequence or genotype the genomes to identify gene variants (such as SNPs) in each group.
Use statistics and bioinformatics to find variants that occur significantly more often in people with dementia.
Follow up with cohort studies to confirm the link.

questions.question: Describe what is meant by the term monoclonal antibody.
questions.answer: Monoclonal antibodies are identical antibodies produced by a single clone of B cells (hybridoma), all specific to one antigen.
steps: A single B cell (plasma cell) produces one specific antibody.
Cloned cells (e.g. hybridomas) produce large numbers of identical antibodies.
Each monoclonal antibody binds to one specific epitope on an antigen.

questions.question: Give one reason why a placebo was used in the donanemab trial.
questions.answer: To provide a control group so that effects of the drug can be compared with no treatment, separating real effects from placebo effects.
steps: A placebo group receives an inactive treatment that looks the same.
Comparing with it shows whether donanemab has a real effect beyond the placebo effect.

questions.question: Explain why lecanemab may result in brain swelling, given that swelling is a symptom of inflammation.
questions.answer: Lecanemab clears amyloid by triggering an immune response, causing inflammation that makes blood vessels leaky so fluid enters brain tissue.
steps: Lecanemab is an antibody that binds amyloid and triggers immune clearance.
This triggers inflammation in the brain, which increases the permeability of blood vessels.
Fluid leaks out of the vessels into the brain tissue, causing swelling (oedema).

questions.question: Suggest one reason why researchers suggest starting drugs even earlier in the disease.
questions.answer: Neurones lost before symptoms appear cannot be replaced, so treatment is most effective before much damage occurs.
steps: Damage to neurones occurs years before symptoms appear.
Once neurones die the damage is irreversible, so early treatment can prevent more loss.

questions.question: Which is a description of a GM organism (options: amplified nucleic acid sequence; organism containing genetic material from another species; virus containing DNA; DNA containing a mutation)?
questions.answer: B an organism containing genetic material from another species
steps: A GM organism has had genes added from another species (transgenic).
The other options describe a PCR product, a virus, and a mutation, not a GM organism.

questions.answer: BVZ binds a specific antigen (VEGF) that cancer cells need, blocking blood vessel growth and marking cells for immune destruction.
steps: BVZ is a monoclonal antibody that binds specifically to VEGF, a growth factor.
Blocking VEGF stops new blood vessels forming, starving the tumour of oxygen and nutrients.
Antibody binding can also mark cells for destruction by immune cells (e.g. by complement or phagocytes).

questions.question: Explain how Ted Turlings and colleagues could have identified that the BtPMaT1 gene in the whitefly was originally a plant gene.

A close match to a plant gene, and lack of similarity to other insect genes, shows it came from a plant.

questions.question: Explain why the frequency of the BtPMaT1 gene increases in the whitefly population.
questions.answer: Individuals with BtPMaT1 gain a survival and reproductive advantage, so they pass the allele on more and its frequency rises.

Over generations the frequency of the allele in the population increases.

questions.answer: Inject a fluorescent (red) protein gene construct into a single-celled zygote, raise the fish, and breed carriers with red fluorescence.

Microinject the construct into a single-celled zebrafish embryo (zygote).

Breed selected transgenic fish, and select homozygous offspring to establish a stable population.

questions.topic: Risks And Benefits Of GM Zebrafish
questions.question: Suggest the risks and benefits of genetically modifying zebrafish.
questions.answer: Benefits include research models and pollution detection; risks include escape into wild populations and ecological or welfare effects.

questions.question: Suggest how the skin cells doubled in size to cover the area of the damage.
questions.answer: Cells increase their cytoplasm and organelles (through increased protein synthesis) and divide by mitosis to cover the wound.
steps: After damage, skin cells increase protein synthesis, enlarging their cytoplasm and organelles.
Cells then move into the wound and divide by mitosis to fill the gap.
This increases the total number of cells over the area of damage.

questions.topic: Single-Celled Embryo Becoming Red Skin Cells
questions.question: Explain how a single-celled zebrafish embryo injected with the colour-producing gene could develop into an adult with red skin cells.
questions.answer: The gene is incorporated into the zygote genome, so mitosis copies it into every cell, and it is expressed in skin cells by their promoter.
steps: The injected gene is inserted into the zygote genome.
Mitosis of the zygote copies the gene into all daughter cells, so every cell carries it.
During development, the gene is switched on in skin cells by the promoter, producing the red pigment protein.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term homeostasis.
questions.answer: Maintenance of a stable internal environment within narrow limits, using negative feedback.
steps: Homeostasis keeps conditions such as blood glucose, temperature and water potential within set limits.
It works through negative feedback, which reverses changes from the set point.
